title: Beyond the Fill by Dr. Biraj Patel
html:
The role of bioceramics and conservative shaping

by Dr. Biraj Patel

Obturation begins long before the master cone is placed. The prepared canal must allow irrigants to reach the apical region while preserving dentin. A postoperative radiograph documents the fill; it does not show whether the entire canal system was disinfected.

In many canals, I aim for a conservative taper (4% or less), adjusted to anatomy rather than applied as a fixed rule. Apical diameter and irrigation access still matter. A narrower shape can preserve radicular dentin and accommodate a fitted cone, but a preparation that prevents effective irrigant delivery is too conservative for that case. Shaping and disinfection have to be planned together.

Hydraulic calcium silicate sealers, often called bioceramics, offer a different way to fill that space. Many are premixed, flow around gutta-percha, and set through a moisture-dependent reaction. Laboratory studies report biocompatibility, high initial alkalinity, dimensional stability, and mineral formation under suitable conditions. These properties do not make up for missed anatomy or incomplete cleaning. Formulations and instructions vary.

This is where single-cone obturation can be useful. A gutta-percha cone matched to the preparation provides the central core; the hydraulic bioceramic sealer flows into the space around it. The technique is straightforward to deliver in narrow or curved canals and avoids enlarging a 4% preparation simply to make room for a heat plugger. It also avoids the wedging forces of compaction. These are practical advantages, not a substitute for disinfection or proof of better healing. I verify apical fit and working length, inject sealer sparingly, and avoid large extrusions. Broad oval spaces or irregular anatomy may call for another approach.

Tooth #30 illustrates these decisions (Figs. 1a–c). It presented with pulp necrosis, a chronic apical abscess, and a sinus tract. A deep existing restoration was a likely contributor to the loss of vitality. No crack was seen on internal inspection. I shaped the mesial canals to 30/.04 and the distal canal to 35/.04 with EdgeFile X7 files, balancing irrigation access with preservation of dentin. Sodium hypochlorite and EDTA were used during treatment, followed by an interappointment calcium hydroxide dressing.

Three cases in one year





Fig. 1a: #30 Before treatment



Fig. 1b: #30 After obturation



Fig. 1c: #30 One year, bony infill


At the four-week visit, the sinus tract had resolved. I completed irrigation and obturated the canals with gutta-percha and EdgeBioCeramic Sealer. A composite core was placed, and the referring general dentist subsequently restored the tooth with a crown. At one year, the follow-up radiograph showed bony infill in the periapical area.

Tooth #18 provides a second example: It was obturated with EdgeUtopia Sealer, and its periapical appearance had improved at one year (Figs. 2a–c). Tooth #21 had a lateral lesion. I instrumented it with EdgeFile X7 files and obturated with EdgeBioCeramic Sealer (Figs. 3a–c). The postoperative radiograph shows sealer within a lateral canal; the one-year film shows improvement in the lateral radiolucency.




Fig. 2a: #18 Before treatment


Fig. 2b: #18 After obturation


Fig. 2c: #18 One year


Fig. 3a: #21 Before treatment


Fig. 3b: #21 After obturation


Fig. 3c: #21 One year


The common thread in these three cases is not the sealer but the sequence behind it: shaping that lets irrigants reach the apical third, preserving dentin where the anatomy allows, and fitting the cone to the canal as it was actually prepared. The hydraulic bioceramic sealer then fills the space around that cone; in #21, sealer is visible within a lateral canal. The one-year images are encouraging, and they reflect cleaning, filling, and restoration working together. The decisions that matter most in obturation are made before the fill.
